title: 'Vitaï Lampada'
description: Published in 1892 and the most famous English poem about the public school: the cricket field as the training ground for the empire.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves from a school cricket match, where a boy holds the game while the fate of the school hangs on the last ball, to a battle in the desert where the same schoolboy, now a soldier, hears his captain's cry of 'Play up! play up! and play the game!' as his regiment breaks.
historical_context: 1892: the English public school cult of games, the imperial campaigns of the 1890s, and the debate on the moral value of sport.
literary_significance: 'Vitaï Lampada' is the most quoted and most parodied poem of the imperial ideal: it fixed the English equation between sport and empire, it became the classic text of the public school ethos, and it is the indispensable document of the mindset that went to war in 1914.

title: The Island Race
description: Published in 1898 and Newbolt's most ambitious imperial collection: the English race, the sea and the imperial mission in verse.
plot_or_argument: The poems celebrate the English as an island race that has become the ruler of the seas, and present English history as a providential mission: Drake, Nelson, the colonial wars and the imperial destiny are all brought into a single story of the race and the flag.
historical_context: 1898: the Diamond Jubilee, the imperial federation movement, the Boer War and the racial ideology of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Island Race is the fullest expression of the imperial idea in English verse: its racial theory of English history made it a central text of imperial ideology, and it is the clearest literary statement of the assumptions that the twentieth century would have to unlearn.

title: Trilby
description: Published in 1894 and the most popular novel of the decade: a tone-deaf artists' model becomes a great singer under the hypnotic power of Svengali.
plot_or_argument: Trilby O'Ferrall, an Irish artists' model in the Latin Quarter, is loved by three English art students; the sinister musician Svengali hypnotises her and makes her a famous singer, she collapses when he dies, and she dies herself soon after, while the pathetic and comic details of bohemian Paris fill the novel.
principal_characters: Trilby O'Ferrall; Svengali; Little Billee; Taffy Wynne; the Laird; Madame Vinard; Gecko; Zouzou
historical_context: 1894: the Paris of the Latin Quarter in the 1850s, the vogue of hypnotism and Mesmerism, the English art student abroad, and the new mass market for the illustrated novel.
literary_significance: Trilby was the most popular novel of the 1890s and one of the first modern best-sellers: it created Svengali and the word 'Svengali', it made the artists' model and bohemian Paris into a popular mythology, and 'Trilby' gave the world the trilby hat, the most successful merchandising event in nineteenth-century publishing.

title: Peter Ibbetson
description: Published in 1891 and du Maurier's strange, haunting first novel: a man in prison dreams his way into a shared world with the woman he has loved since childhood.
plot_or_argument: Peter Ibbetson, an architect imprisoned for murder, discovers that he can enter the dreams of the Duchess of Towers, his childhood love, and that in the dream world the two of them can live an entire life together, until the dream becomes more real than the prison and death becomes the final reunion.
principal_characters: Peter Ibbetson; the Duchess of Towers; Mr Ibbetson; Mrs Ibbetson; Colonel Ibbetson; Griffiths; Mrs Glynne
historical_context: 1891: the Society for Psychical Research and the new study of dreams, the Victorian interest in telepathy, and the aesthetic cult of the childhood romance.
literary_significance: Peter Ibbetson is the most original English novel of the 1890s and the founding text of the modern dream-romance: its invention of a shared dream-world made it a source for the twentieth-century fantastic novel, and its combination of Victorian sentiment and oneiric invention has never been imitated successfully.

title: The Martian
description: Published posthumously in 1897 and du Maurier's last novel: an artist's double life and the visionary guardian he calls the Martian.
plot_or_argument: Barty Josselin, a brilliant and erratic English artist, is guided through his life by a supernatural presence he calls the Martian, who first appears to him as a child and who dictates his most successful novel; the book follows his loves, his career and his death, in a strange mixture of comic memoir and spiritual fantasy.
historical_context: 1896-97: the aesthetic movement's last years, the Society for Psychical Research, and the Victorian interest in the guardian spirit and the automatic writer.
literary_significance: The Martian is the strangest of du Maurier's books and the last major novel of the aesthetic movement: its fantasy of the guardian spirit and its comic memoir of the artistic life made it a cult novel, and it is the link between Trilby and the twentieth-century fantastic fiction.

title: The Prisoner of Zenda
description: Published in 1894 and the founding Ruritanian romance: an Englishman impersonates the king of a small European state on the day of his coronation.
plot_or_argument: Rudolf Rassendyll, an English gentleman on holiday, discovers he is the double of the King of Ruritania; when the king is drugged by his half-brother Black Michael, Rudolf takes his place at the coronation, falls in love with the Princess Flavia, and finally rescues the king from the castle of Zenda in a swordfight with Rupert of Hentzau.
principal_characters: Rudolf Rassendyll; Rudolf V; Princess Flavia; Black Michael; Rupert of Hentzau; Colonel Sapt; Fritz von Tarlenheim; Antoinette de Mauban
historical_context: 1894: the small states of central Europe, the English gentleman's code of honour, the vogue of the adventure romance after Stevenson, and the imperial self-image of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Prisoner of Zenda invented the Ruritanian romance and created one of the most durable formulas in popular fiction: it has never been out of print, it gave the language the word 'Ruritanian', and it has been filmed, staged and imitated continuously for more than a century.

title: Rupert of Hentzau
description: Published in 1898 and the darker sequel to The Prisoner of Zenda: the return of the villain and the death of the hero.
plot_or_argument: Three years after Zenda, Rupert of Hentzau returns to Ruritania to pursue Queen Flavia; Rudolf Rassendyll is drawn back to the country to defend her, and the novel ends with his death in a duel with Rupert and the queen's lifelong widowhood.
principal_characters: Rupert of Hentzau; Rudolf Rassendyll; Queen Flavia; Colonel Sapt; Fritz von Tarlenheim; Rosa Holf; Bauer; Bernenstein
historical_context: 1898: the imperial adventure vogue, the honour code of the English gentleman, and the popular appetite for the sequel.
literary_significance: Rupert of Hentzau is the rare sequel that surpasses the original in seriousness: its ending — the death of the hero and the renunciation of love — gave the Ruritanian romance a tragic dimension, and it is the finest of Hope's adventure novels.

title: The Dolly Dialogues
description: Published in 1894 and the wittiest English society dialogue of the decade: a series of conversations between a young man and the woman he does not quite marry.
plot_or_argument: The dialogues follow Sam Carter and the beautiful, imperious Dolly Mickleham through the drawing rooms, racecourses and country houses of the 1890s, in conversations that turn on flirtation, marriage, money and the small absurdities of English society, and that end with Dolly marrying someone else and Sam accepting it gracefully.
historical_context: 1893-94: the London season of the 1890s, the daily press and the dialogue sketch, and the English vogue for the light comedy of manners.
literary_significance: The Dolly Dialogues is the finest English dialogue sequence of the 1890s and one of the wittiest books of the period: its style and its irony make it the English equivalent of the French maxim, and it is the book by which Hope's contemporaries rated him above the Zenda romances.

title: The God in the Car
description: Published in 1894 and Hope's most serious novel: a financial adventurer builds an African empire and loses the woman he loves.
plot_or_argument: Tommy Vosse, a brilliant and unscrupulous financier, builds a railway and a mining concession in Africa and becomes the maker of an empire; he loves Maggie Dennison, who marries another man, and the novel follows his rise, his manipulation of the press and the government, and his final loneliness at the height of his power.
historical_context: 1894: the scramble for Africa, the mining finance of the 1890s, the Jameson Raid and the imperial adventurers, and the English debate on the ethics of speculation.
literary_significance: The God in the Car is the finest English novel of imperial finance: its portrait of the empire-builder and its analysis of the relation between money, press and politics made it the most serious of Hope's books, and it is a key text of the English literature of the scramble for Africa.

title: 'The Monkey's Paw'
description: Published in 1902 and the most famous English horror story of the century: a mummified paw grants three wishes, and the third is made in terror.
plot_or_argument: Mr White, an old soldier's friend, takes the monkey's paw that grants three wishes; the first brings the money they need at the cost of their son's death in a factory accident, the second is a wish for the son's return, and when the knocking comes at the door in the night the third wish sends it away again.
principal_characters: Mr White; Mrs White; Herbert White; Sergeant-Major Morris
historical_context: 1902: the English suburban household of the 1900s, the vogue of the oriental talisman, and the taste for the short supernatural story after Kipling and James.
literary_significance: 'The Monkey's Paw' is the most famous English horror story ever written and the most anthologised: its cold economy, its suburban setting and its implication rather than display made it the model for the modern horror story, and it is a permanent part of the English ghost-story tradition.

title: Many Cargoes
description: Published in 1896 and Jacobs's first collection: comic stories of the London docks, the barges and the riverside.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow the bargees, the night watchmen, the sailors and their wives through the small disasters of working life — a cargo lost, a wife deceived, a windfall squandered, a ghost that turns out to be a fellow — each told in the exact speech of the London riverside and each with a twist at the end.
historical_context: 1896: the London docks and the Thames barges, the working-class household of the 1890s, and the magazine market for the short comic story.
literary_significance: Many Cargoes established Jacobs as the finest English comic short-story writer of his generation: its dialogue and its construction are models of the form, and it founded the series of collections that made him the most popular humorous writer of the early twentieth century.

title: The Lady of the Barge
description: Published in 1902 and the collection containing 'The Monkey's Paw': the best of Jacobs's comic and supernatural stories.
plot_or_argument: The collection mixes the riverside comedies of marriage and money with 'The Monkey's Paw' and other tales of the uncanny, and shows both of Jacobs's gifts — the comic twist and the cold horror — in a single volume.
historical_context: 1902: the London and Kent riverside, the Edwardian suburban household, and the magazine fiction of the 1900s.
literary_significance: The Lady of the Barge is Jacobs's finest collection and the book that contains both his masterpiece of horror and his best comic stories: it shows the technical range that made him a model for the English short story, and it is a classic of the late-Victorian and Edwardian short story.

title: Night Watches
description: Published in 1914 and the last of Jacobs's great collections: the night watchman and the riverside household in the years before the war.
plot_or_argument: The stories are told by or around a night watchman at the docks, and follow the small comedies of the working household: the lodger, the wife's relations, the legacy, the misunderstanding, the ghost that is only a fellow-worker in a white sheet.
historical_context: 1914: the London docks before the First World War, the working-class household of the 1900s, and the last years of the comic magazine.
literary_significance: Night Watches is the finest of Jacobs's later collections and the culmination of his comic art: its dialogue and its construction are as precise as ever, and it is the collection in which the English riverside comedy reaches its fullest expression.

title: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical
description: Tennyson's first solo collection, published in 1830 when he was twenty, and the volume that announced an art of pure sensation: 'Claribel', 'Mariana', 'The Kraken', 'The Poet' and the elegiac 'Ode to Memory' are the poems by which it is known.
plot_or_argument: The volume's poems are lyric and meditative rather than narrative: 'Mariana' fixes a woman in a moated grange in a single endlessly repeated condition; 'The Kraken' sleeps in the abysm of the deep; 'The Poet' describes the poet's mind as a world; 'Recollections of the Arabian Nights' builds a dream palace from pure sound.
historical_context: The 1830 volume appeared in the year of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway and of the July Revolution; it was reviewed by Arthur Henry Hallam in the Englishman's Magazine as the work of a new school of poetry whose interest lay in the 'originality' of its feeling for nature and its 'descriptive' power.
literary_significance: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical introduced the 'Tennysonian' manner that dominated English verse for the next sixty years: the picture of a state of mind held in a landscape, and the perfection of sound. It is also the volume in which the Cambridge circle of the Apostles found its poet.

title: Poems (1832)
description: The 1832 volume (dated 1833) containing 'The Lady of Shalott', 'The Palace of Art', 'Oenone', 'The Lotos-Eaters' and 'A Dream of Fair Women' — the volume attacked by John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review in 1833, and the one whose ten years of revision produced the 1842 Poems.
plot_or_argument: The poems are symbolic narratives: the Lady of Shalott weaves a mirror-image of the world until the curse falls on her; the Palace of Art is a soul's self-built retreat which decays; the Lotos-Eaters turn Homeric episode into a moral argument for withdrawal and oblivion; Oenone speaks the wrongs of Helen from the mountain.
historical_context: The 1830s, the Quarterly Review's hostility to the 'Cockney' school and to Tennyson as an example of poetic obscurity, and the deaths that darkened the decade (Hallam in 1833, Tennyson's brother Charles's family troubles).
literary_significance: This is the volume that gave the Victorian age its central myths: the enclosed lady, the palace of art and the island of the lotos-eaters became permanent figures for the artist's relation to the world, and the 1832 text's 'obscurity' became the test case for the Victorian debate about difficulty in poetry.

title: Poems (1842)
description: The two-volume Poems of 1842 that ended the ten years' silence: the revised versions of the 1830 and 1832 poems together with 'Morte d'Arthur', 'Locksley Hall', 'Ulysses', 'The Two Voices', 'The Vision of Sin' and 'Break, break, break'.
plot_or_argument: The volume's new poems are dramatic and sententious: 'Ulysses' is a monologue of heroic endurance, 'Locksley Hall' a young man's prophecy of the coming age, 'Morte d'Arthur' a fragment of the planned Arthurian epic, and 'The Two Voices' a debate between despair and the will to live.
historical_context: The ten years in which Tennyson revised, lost Hallam and his friend Edward Fitzgerald's milieu, and battled poverty; the 1842 publication made him the leading poet of his generation and freed him from dependence.
literary_significance: The 1842 Poems established the Victorian canon of Tennyson: it is the volume on which his contemporary fame rested, and 'Ulysses', 'Morte d'Arthur' and 'Locksley Hall' became the texts by which Victorian England understood heroism, chivalry and the future.

title: The Princess: A Medley
description: Published in 1847 (revised 1850, 1851, 1853, with the intercalated songs added in 1850), a serio-comic poem on the higher education of women: a prince disguises himself as a maid to enter a women's college founded by the princess he is betrothed to.
plot_or_argument: Prince Gama's son, betrothed in childhood to the Princess Ida, enters her college in disguise with his friends; discovered, he is wounded, nursed, and the college collapses when Ida's heart is touched by the story of a mother's love; the poem ends with the prince's vision of a reconciled relation between the sexes and with the lyric 'Now sleeps the crimson petal'.
narrative_structure: A prologue and conclusion frame seven cantos of narrative, with six interspersed songs; in blank verse with lyrical interludes.
principal_characters: the Prince; Princess Ida; Cyril; Florian; Psyche; King Gama; the Lady Blanche; Melissa
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the narrative; the songs in various lyric stanzas ('Tears, idle tears' in a four-line stanza with refrain).
historical_context: The 1840s debate on women's education (Queen's College, London, 1848; the Governesses' Benevolent Institution), the early feminist argument of the English Woman's Journal, and the poem's later embarrassment to its author as the 'woman question' became serious.
literary_significance: The Princess is the Victorian poem on women's education and the most ambitious attempt in verse to argue the case for female intellectual life. Its mixture of comic and serious registers, and its interpolated songs, made it a permanent anthology source, and its reception shows the shift in the debate from comedy to politics inside a single decade.

title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
description: The great elegy of the nineteenth century, begun on the death of Arthur Henry Hallam in Vienna on 15 September 1833 and printed privately in 1849 and published in May 1850: 131 lyric sections in a single stanza, moving from raw grief through the geological and religious crisis of the mid-1840s to a hard-won faith in the 'one far-off divine event'.
plot_or_argument: The sequence is not narrative but seasonal and argumentative: it opens with the yew tree and the funeral, moves through the first Christmas, the springs and winters of the following years, the letter from the widow of Hallam's father, the vision of nature as 'red in tooth and claw', the vision of Hallam as a type of the perfected man, and ends with the marriage of Tennyson's sister Cecilia and Edmund Lushington and a benediction on the child to come.
narrative_structure: 131 numbered sections of three or four stanzas, grouped by the anniversaries of Hallam's death and by the seasons; a prologue and an epilogue (the marriage of Cecilia Tennyson).
literary_form: Elegiac sequence in 131 sections and a prologue and epilogue; 'A. H. H.' = Arthur Henry Hallam
meter_and_prosody: The In Memoriam stanza: iambic tetrameter rhymed abba, a closed, echoing quatrain that became the standard English elegiac measure.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s: the Oxford Movement, the geology of Lyell and the 'Vestiges' controversy, the crisis of faith, and the private world of the Tennyson family at Somersby and High Beach; the poem's theology is Broad Church and its science is the new geology.
literary_significance: In Memoriam is the central poem of Victorian doubt and the one work in which the age's scientific and religious crisis is dramatised at full length. It gave the language 'nature, red in tooth and claw' and 'the ringing grooves of change', and its stanza (the 'In Memoriam stanza', abba) became the standard elegiac form of the century. Queen Victoria told Tennyson it was her consolation after the death of Prince Albert.

title: Maud, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1855 and Tennyson's own favourite among his long poems: a monodrama in a variety of metres spoken by a young man driven to madness and murder by his father's ruin, the love of Maud, and the Crimean War.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, ruined by a fraudulent lawsuit against his father, falls in love with Maud, the daughter of his father's enemy; her brother opposes the match, the lovers are discovered, the speaker kills Maud's brother in a duel, and goes mad, imagining himself dead; the poem ends with his recovery and his departure for the Crimean War.
principal_characters: the unnamed speaker; Maud; Maud's brother; Maud's father; the speaker's father
meter_and_prosody: Eleven sections in varied metres, from lyric tetrameters to a prose-like dramatic speech, with refrains and song fragments.
historical_context: The 1850s: the financial fraud of the period, the 'Maud mania' of the poem's reception, and above all the Crimean War (1853-56), which the poem's ending consecrates as a national redemption.
literary_significance: Maud is the most modern and the most disturbing of Tennyson's long poems: its unstable speaker, its abrupt metrical shifts and its treatment of sexual hysteria and financial ruin make it a key text for the study of Victorian masculinity, and its war ending gave the poem its contemporary scandal. Modern criticism has made it the most discussed of the poems after In Memoriam.

title: Idylls of the King
description: Tennyson's Arthurian epic, published in instalments over twenty-six years — 'Enid' and 'Elaine' (as 'Enid and Nimue') in 1859, 'The Holy Grail' in 1869, 'Gareth and Lynette' and 'The Last Tournament' in 1872, 'Balin and Balan' in 1885 — and dedicated to the memory of Prince Albert.
plot_or_argument: The twelve idylls trace the rise and fall of Arthur's order: the coming of Arthur and the founding of the Round Table; the individual knights' vows and failures (Gareth, Balin, Geraint and Enid, Lancelot, Percivale); the quest of the Holy Grail, which breaks the fellowship; the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere; the rebellion of Mordred and the last battle; and Arthur's passing to Avilion.
principal_characters: Arthur; Guinevere; Lancelot; Elaine; Enid; Geraint; Vivien; Merlin; Mordred; Percivale; Galahad; Balin; Balan; Gareth; Lynette; Bedivere
literary_form: Arthurian epic in twelve idylls, in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse in the idyll form; each idyll a self-contained narrative episode with its own moral.
historical_context: The Victorian revival of Arthurian matter (the 1839 Eglinton Tournament, the Pre-Raphaelite Arthurian paintings, Malory reprinted in 1817), the empire and its moral mission, and the death of Prince Albert in 1861, which gave the poem a national resonance.
literary_significance: The Idylls are the Victorian age's central myth of empire and of its corruption from within. They made Malory's Arthur a national possession and provided the moral vocabulary of Victorian chivalry, while the poem's increasingly pessimistic later books gave the twentieth century its image of the Victorian imperial self-doubt.

title: Enoch Arden, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1864 and sold 17,000 copies on the day of publication: the story of a fisherman cast away for ten years who returns to find his wife remarried, together with 'The Northern Farmer' dialect poems and 'Aylmer's Field'.
plot_or_argument: Enoch Arden is shipwrecked and lives alone on a desert island for more than ten years; rescued, he returns to find his wife Annie married to his rival Philip, and conceals himself until his death, having provided for her. The volume also includes 'The Northern Farmer, Old Style' and 'New Style', dialect monologues, and 'Aylmer's Field', a narrative of avarice and vengeance.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for Enoch Arden; the Lincolnshire dialect poems in rhymed couplets and rural measures.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Victorian taste for the narrative poem as family reading, the Lincolnshire dialect of Tennyson's boyhood, and the emigration and shipwreck narratives of the period.
literary_significance: Enoch Arden was the most popular narrative poem of the century and the type of the Victorian verse tale read aloud in the home; it also contains the dialect poems that make Tennyson one of the earliest serious users of regional English speech in verse, a technique taken up by William Barnes and by the twentieth-century regional poets.

title: The Holy Grail and Other Poems
description: Published in 1869, containing 'The Holy Grail', 'The Coming of Arthur', 'The Passing of Arthur' and 'Pelleas and Ettarre': the volume in which the Arthurian epic was given its spiritual centre and its frame.
plot_or_argument: 'The Holy Grail' narrates the Grail vision and the quest that breaks the Round Table, told by Percivale to a monk; 'The Coming of Arthur' establishes the founding myth; 'The Passing of Arthur' narrates the last battle and Bedivere's return of Excalibur.
historical_context: The 1860s and the Victorian fascination with the Grail (the 1869 volume coincided with the Pre-Raphaelite and Wagnerian treatments), the religious doubt of the period and the poem's answer in the vision granted only to the pure.
literary_significance: 'The Holy Grail' is the supreme Victorian treatment of the Grail legend and the moment at which the Idylls became a sustained critique of spiritual ambition as a force that dissolves human community; it is also the poem in which Tennyson's blank verse reaches its most incantatory.

title: Becket
description: Published in 1884 and performed at the Lyceum Theatre by Henry Irving on 6 February 1884: Tennyson's most successful play, on the conflict of Henry II and Thomas Becket.
plot_or_argument: Becket, the king's chancellor turned archbishop, resists Henry's attempt to subject the Church to the royal courts; the conflict over criminous clerks, the exile in France, the return and the murder in the cathedral of 29 December 1170 form the play's structure, and Becket's death is presented as a martyrdom accepted in advance.
historical_context: The 1880s and the disestablishment question, the Oxford Movement's legacy, and the Victorian stage's revival of verse drama under Irving and Ellen Terry.
literary_significance: Becket is the best of Tennyson's late plays and one of the few Victorian verse tragedies to hold the stage; it revived the historical verse drama in England and prepared the way for the poetic theatre of the 1890s and of Yeats.

title: Crossing the Bar
description: Written in October 1889, three years before the poet's death, and printed as the final poem of every collected edition: a prayer for a calm passage at the boundary of life and death, with the Pilot face to face.
plot_or_argument: A short meditation spoken at the moment of departure: the speaker hopes for a tide 'too full for sound and foam', asks that no sadness attend his crossing, and ends with the hope of meeting his 'Pilot face to face'.
historical_context: Tennyson's old age, his friendship with the poem's occasion (a crossing of the Solent), and the Victorian funeral culture that made the poem a standard part of the burial service.
literary_significance: 'Crossing the Bar' is the most quoted Victorian deathbed poem and the model for the short terminal lyric of the twentieth century; its 'Pilot' image gave the age a consoling figure for providence that survives in the language.

title: Pauline: A Fragment of a Confession
description: Published anonymously at the author's expense in 1833 when he was twenty-one, and withdrawn by him in later life: the confession of a young poet to the woman he loves, tracing his search for a faith through Shelleyan idealism, nature and art.
plot_or_argument: The speaker addresses Pauline across a blank-verse monologue in which he recounts his childhood, his worship of Shelley, his loss of faith, and his discovery that love for her gives him a centre; the poem ends with a vow of fidelity.
historical_context: The 1830s, the Shelley cult, Byron's death and the decline of the 'Satanic' school, and the young Browning's reading of Shelley, Keats and the French memoirists.
literary_significance: Pauline is the earliest fully developed dramatic monologue in English in Browning's hand, and its confessional method — a speaker who reveals more than he knows — is the prototype of all his later work.
